subject: GPU runway, burst sensitivity and egress cost audit

Cc: ops@embercloud.com
Date: 2028-01-10T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Throughput targets & burst cost modelling for private GPU pool

Hi Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo last week. We had a quick exec ask to validate whether a private GPU pool (VPC-hosted, single-tenant) can hit the following targets before we proceed to procurement:

- Steady-state throughput: 1,800 concurrent short-chat requests (avg prompt+response tokens ~120) at p95 <= 250ms
- Burst absorb: sustained 6,000 qps for up to 10 minutes with graceful degradation (queueing or reduced max tokens)
- Cost sensitivity: expected egress and token cost delta vs hosted baseline (we're particularly concerned about egress and KMS traffic charges)

Can Redwood provide a short runbook and a cost/runway estimate (engineering assumptions + attachments welcome) so we can present this to finance next week?

Also useful: our region will be us-west1, and we expect 80% of traffic to be chat with short-turnaround reranking.

-Alex
Alex Ruiz
Head of Platform Engineering, EmberCloud
ops@embercloud.com

PS: if you could include a simple admission-control knob suggestion (e.g., concurrency caps per shard) that would be perfect.

From: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Throughput targets & burst cost modelling for private GPU pool

Alex —

Thanks for the clear brief. Attaching a short runway workbook and a private-deploy runbook that outline assumptions and a simple admission-control recipe. Highlights below:

- Steady-state: to achieve 1,800 concurrent short-chat QPS at p95 <= 250ms we recommend a starting pool of 16 A100-equivalent GPUs running a bfloat16-quantized 70B model split across 4 shards (continuous batching, warm KV cache). Assumption: average decode tokens per request = 30, internal batching efficiency 2.2x.
- Burst absorb: for a 6,000 qps 10-minute sustained window we propose a warm standby of +10 GPUs (burst pool) and an admission-control horizon that shifts non-critical requests into a low-priority queue after 2s. This gives ~90% success for priority traffic and controlled tail latency degradation.
- Network/Egress: estimated egress delta vs hosted ~+0.6c per request (model outputs larger than inputs). KMS calls add negligible cost per call but add latency; recommend client-side caching of keys where policy allows.
- Operational knobs: per-shard concurrency limit, request weight routing (short vs long), and automatic scale-down cooldown of 8m to avoid churn.

Attachments: sizing-runway.xlsx (workbook), privdeploy-runbook.pdf (runbook).

I'll loop Jonas for a simulation snapshot and a CSV of the burst simulation.

—Marissa

Alex / team —

Following up with the simulation outputs and a few low-level notes. See attached burst-sim.csv for a minute-by-minute QPS->latency trace (synthetic, based on your token distribution). Key technical tradeoffs:

1) Warm KV cache: warm-cache hit rate is the single biggest driver of p95. Cold starts add ~60–120ms per request depending on model size. We simulate 95% hit after warmup; plan to warm the most common prefixes.

2) Continuous batching vs immediate dispatch: at 1,800 concurrent short requests batching gives us ~2.1x token throughput improvement but increases median by ~40ms; with the p95 target you can tune batching threshold to 30ms window to retain latency envelope.

3) Admission control curve (recommended):
   - soft_limit = 1,900 concurrent short requests (start shedding non-critical at 1,900)
   - hard_limit = 2,500 (reject non-priority)
   - burst_pool_scale = add 10 warm GPUs at ~4,500 concurrent short requests

4) Egress and network: measured egress for model outputs average 3.2 KB per request; at your traffic profile in us-west1 that maps to ~1.1 TB/day during a 6k-qps sustained window. We estimate egress billing and cross-region replication if enabled; add explicit buffer to runway.

5) Failure modes and mitigation: preemptible GPU risks — prefer dedicated reserved instances for burst pool; set fallback to a smaller quantized variant with identical API surface to avoid client changes.

I'll highlight a few rows in the CSV showing the minute where p95 crosses 250ms and the corresponding queued backlog. If helpful we can run a short PoC on your staging VPC to validate network egress and kernel warmup times (1–2 day spike test).

-Jonas
Jonas Weber
